introduces.def: A single, tiny, exact action for the computer to carry out - like setting a value or adding two numbers.
An ordered list of instructions; change the order and you change what it does.
The values a program works on, held in memory.
The part of the computer that runs instructions, fetching and carrying out one at a time, billions of times a second.
A tool that translates the code you write into the tiny instructions the CPU understands.
The computer's fast working memory, where a program and its data must be before the CPU can run them.
The loop the CPU repeats forever: fetch the next instruction from memory, carry it out, repeat.
The CPU's bookmark - it remembers which instruction comes next.
An instruction that changes the program counter to a different line instead of the next one, which is how loops and choices work.
The program in charge of the machine - it launches your program and manages it while it runs.
The part of the operating system that copies a program from storage into memory so it can run.
The place where a program starts running - the first instruction the operating system hands to the CPU.
The routine a program starts from, usually named Main.
A running program, loaded into its own separate patch of memory.
One worker inside the CPU; a single core does one instruction at a time.
Giving one core to several processes in turn, switching thousands of times a second so they seem to run at once.
The part of the operating system that decides which process gets the core next.
Running things at the very same instant on more than one core.
Walling each process off in its own memory so one cannot read or wreck another's, which keeps a crash contained.
The smallest piece of information - a single value that is either 0 (off) or 1 (on).
Counting with only 0s and 1s; every number is a pattern of on and off bits.
A group of eight bits, enough for 256 different values - the unit memory and file sizes are measured in.
An agreed code that maps each thing to a number and back - it decides whether a number means a letter, a colour, or a sound.
One tiny coloured dot of an image, its colour stored as amounts of red, green and blue.
One measurement of a sound wave's height, taken thousands of times a second.
A named bundle of bytes on storage, which you can find again by its name.
A named group of files, arranged in a tree you walk to reach a file.
The rules the operating system checks before it lets a program open or change a file.
A piece of hardware - keyboard, screen, printer, network - that programs reach only by asking the operating system.
The tiny numeric instructions a CPU runs directly - the only language it truly understands.
Human-friendly words and rules for writing programs, which a tool then translates for the machine.
A language close to human ideas rather than raw machine instructions, so one line stands for many CPU steps.
The exact rules for how code must be written in a language.
A named slot in memory that holds a value you can read and change.
The kind of a value - number, text, true/false - which decides what you can do with it.
One complete instruction - a single step the program takes.
A piece of code that produces a value, like 2 + 3 working out to 5.
Writing a computed value into a variable, done with the = operator.
A symbol like + or = that combines or acts on values.
A yes/no question the program asks, like temp > 10, that works out to true or false.
Choosing between paths - run one block when a condition is true, another when it is false.
Repeating steps by jumping back to check a condition again, so you write them once instead of many times.
A named bundle of steps you can call and reuse, with inputs and an output.
A named input a function receives, which arrives as a local variable when the function is called.
The result a function hands back to whatever called it.
A variable that exists only while its function is running.
A mistake in the code - the computer did what you wrote, not what you meant.
Code that breaks the language's rules, which the compiler catches before the program runs.
Valid code that runs but does the wrong thing, like using minus where you meant plus.
Stepping through code line by line, watching the values, to find where it goes wrong.
The number of a memory slot, which lets the program find that exact slot again.
The memory region for the values a function is using right now, where each call adds a frame on top that is removed automatically when the call ends.
The memory region for objects that must outlive the call that made them, kept until nothing refers to them.
The part that reclaims heap memory once nothing points to an object any more.
A property of RAM: it is fast to reach but wiped the moment power drops.
A type whose variable holds the data itself, so copying it duplicates the value.
A type whose variable holds the address of an object on the heap, so copying it duplicates only the address.
A value that is a memory address - follow it to reach the real object.
The phase before a program runs, when the compiler translates the source and checks the rules.
The phase when the built program actually executes, one instruction at a time.
A rule-breaking mistake the compiler catches at compile time, before anything runs.
A platform that finishes and runs a portable build on each machine, like .NET.
Building on one machine but aiming the compiler at a different target - another CPU or operating system.
Non-volatile hardware that keeps data after a program stops and after the power is off.
Keeping data past the end of a program by saving it to storage, and loading it back later.
A file on disk is an inode - its bytes plus facts about them like size, time, and who can read it - reached through a name in a folder.
The wires and wireless links that let one program talk to another, even across the world.
The program that asks for something over a network.
The program that answers requests over a network.
A message a client sends asking for something.
The answer a server sends back.
The set list of things a server offers and how to ask for them - like a menu.
Ready-made code someone else wrote and shared, which you call instead of writing it yourself.
The big set of built-in tools every language ships with, ready the moment you start.
A bundle of code someone published for others to reuse, fetched and added to your project.
A tool that fetches the packages you ask for, installs the right versions, and pulls in their dependencies.
A package your program relies on, which may rely on further packages of its own.
A tool that tracks every change to your code, so you never lose work and can see what changed and when.
A saved snapshot of your code at a moment worth keeping, with a short message describing the change.
The timeline of all commits - how the code grew, snapshot by snapshot.
Several people working on one project, each committing their own changes without overwriting each other.
